bloodPressure.label: Blood pressure
bloodPressure.howToMeasure: Sit secured to your seat, rest for 5 minutes, and use the arm monitor. Enter both numbers.
bloodPressure.whyMeasure: Without gravity, body fluids shift toward the head. In eight astronauts, all men, average 24-hour inflight blood pressure was 8 mmHg lower systolic and 9 mmHg lower diastolic than on the ground, with unchanged heart rate. The study does not define a safe range for an individual.

heartRate.label: Heart rate
heartRate.howToMeasure: Measure at rest, before exercising. Use the finger oximeter, a wearable sensor, or count your pulse for 1 minute.
heartRate.whyMeasure: Microgravity changes circulation. Resting heart rate is a simple sign of how your heart is responding.

temperature.label: Temperature
temperature.howToMeasure: Use the onboard thermometer at the same time each day and away from exercise.
temperature.whyMeasure: Spaceflight stress can affect the body's defenses and reactivate dormant viruses. Fever is one early sign.

glucose.label: Blood glucose
glucose.howToMeasure: Measure while fasting with the finger-stick meter, before your first meal.
glucose.whyMeasure: Sentinela includes glucose because the challenge mentions blood sugar, and only selected profiles track it. We found no routine inflight glucose monitoring in the NASA sources reviewed. This does not rule out research or individual indications, or make glucose a measure of adequate nutrition.

sleepHours.label: Sleep
sleepHours.howToMeasure: Enter how many hours you slept during your most recent rest period, not time spent awake in the sleeping bag. If you use a wearable sleep sensor, copy the hours it recorded.
sleepHours.whyMeasure: The crew sees about 16 sunrises a day on the station, which can confuse the body clock. Too little sleep reduces alertness.

mood.label: Mood
mood.howToMeasure: Choose the face that best describes how you felt for most of the day.
mood.whyMeasure: Isolation, confinement, and distance from Earth can weigh on people over time. Tracking the trend helps the crew act early.

stress.label: Stress
stress.howToMeasure: Choose the number that best describes your stress for most of the day.
stress.whyMeasure: On the station, NASA asks astronauts to rate stress in the Reaction Self Test. A study of 24 astronauts linked sleeping 6 hours or less with higher stress.

workload.label: Workload
workload.howToMeasure: Choose the number that best describes today's workload.
workload.whyMeasure: Work overload is part of NASA's risk for poor sleep and irregular schedules. Tracking workload helps the commander redistribute tasks before fatigue builds up.

exerciseMinutes.label: Exercise
exerciseMinutes.howToMeasure: Enter today's minutes of aerobic exercise (running, cycling, rowing) and resistance training (against a load or resistance, such as squats), using your spacecraft's equipment. The app adds them up. Use 0 if you skipped one of them.
exerciseMinutes.whyMeasure: Microgravity affects bones and muscles. NASA reports an average loss of 1% to 1.5% per month in weight-bearing bones in 4- to 6-month missions; this does not predict your loss. Aerobic and resistance exercise are part of the countermeasures, according to your individual plan.

radiationDose.label: Radiation
radiationDose.howToMeasure: Read today's accumulated dose on your personal dosimeter and enter the value in microsieverts.
radiationDose.whyMeasure: Space radiation increases lifetime cancer risk. For scale, the Radi-N2 detector measured about 150 µSv per day of neutrons alone on the station.

bodyMassKg.label: Body mass
bodyMassKg.howToMeasure: Use the spacecraft's weighing equipment, preferably at the same time and under the same conditions, and enter the value in kilograms.
bodyMassKg.whyMeasure: Body mass helps track nutrition and adaptation to flight. The value is compared with mass at the start of the mission.

vision.label: Vision
vision.howToMeasure: Read the near-vision card with one eye at a time and compare it with what you saw at the start of the mission.
vision.whyMeasure: On long ISS missions, about 70% show early signs detectable by optical coherence tomography. A 2023 NASA brief reports optic disc edema in 16% during or after long missions; the criteria differ. This self-report does not diagnose SANS or replace an eye examination.

medication.label: Medication
medication.howToMeasure: Mark each dose scheduled for today that you have taken. Any unmarked dose counts as not taken.
medication.whyMeasure: There is no rapid resupply far from Earth, and the body changes during flight. Recording each dose helps the onboard medical officer know whether the treatment is being followed.

symptoms.label: Symptoms
symptoms.howToMeasure: Mark everything you felt today. If you did not feel anything, continue without marking.
symptoms.whyMeasure: Far from Earth, recording a symptom early gives the crew time to act with onboard resources.

mind.label: Mind and sleep
mind.description: Sleep, mood, stress, workload, and reaction time

station.label: Station
station.description: Low Earth orbit, inside the magnetosphere.

transit.label: Transit
transit.signalDelayLabel: increases with distance (2 min in this demo)

moon.label: Moon
moon.description: Lunar surface, with one-sixth of Earth's gravity.

mars.label: Mars
mars.description: Martian surface, with ground response times of up to 20 minutes.
mars.signalDelayLabel: 3 to 22 min (12 min in this demo)

reactionTime.label: Reaction time
reactionTime.howToMeasure: Take the test somewhere quiet. When the signal appears, tap the area or press Space as fast as you can. Do not respond before the signal. The full test takes 3 minutes.
reactionTime.whyMeasure: NASA's Reaction Self Test tracks attention and performance. This test is a demo and has not been validated as equivalent; the time also depends on the device and the interaction. A single result does not diagnose fatigue or prove fitness.

conditioning.label: Physical conditioning
conditioning.howToMeasure: Complete the periodic assessment defined by the medical team and enter the result as a percentage of the preflight value, along with the apparatus used.
conditioning.whyMeasure: NASA operational guidance recommends maintaining at least 80% of preflight aerobic capacity and strength. This record does not replace a fitness assessment.

resistanceMinutes.label: Resistance training
resistanceMinutes.howToMeasure: Minutes of training against a load or resistance, entered in the exercise step.
resistanceMinutes.whyMeasure: Resistance training protects bones the most in flight. On its own, it reduces bone loss but does not prevent it.

wearable.label: Wearable sensor
wearable.example: e.g. an actigraphy wristband, like the one used on Artemis II

dosimeter.label: Personal dosimeter
dosimeter.example: e.g. an active dosimeter carried in a pocket, as on Artemis II
